item.title: Chinese micro-dramas race onto global stage
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-25
CHONGQING, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- By 10 a.m., a film and animation park in southwest China's Chongqing Municipality is already buzzing with activity. Crews are scattered across their respective sets -- interrogation lights snap on inside a "police station" soundstage, while upstairs in a "hospital ward," a nurse slowly pushes a medicine cart down the corridor. Repurposed from a disused commercial property, the park in the Liangjiang New Area now hosts nearly 300 realistic filming sets and accommodates about 1,000 productions a year, turning out more than 700 short-form dramas annually. A 40-episode micro-drama can be wrapped up in as little as four days. "You can literally show up with just a script," said Zeng Li, head of the park. The facility provides lighting, equipment, costumes, props and extras, alongside accommodation and catering, a turnkey package that allows crews to hit the ground running. With everything under one roof, productions can move seamlessly between scenes, significantly boosting overall efficiency. "Micro-dramas are all about emotional resonance," director Bao Yinfei said, noting that unlike traditional TV series, micro-dramas feature fewer setups, more plot twists and faster pacing, allowing them to grab viewers' attention in a matter of seconds. "This storytelling style transcends language and geographical boundaries. If the story resonates, it can travel." "This production model has pushed every link in the chain, from filming and editing to acting, to pick up the pace, giving rise to a standardized and streamlined ecosystem for micro-drama production in China," Bao added. What's happening in Chongqing is not an isolated case -- it reflects a broader phenomenon reshaping the global entertainment landscape. Made-in-China micro-dramas, with their cliffhanger-packed storytelling and hyper-efficient shoots, have evolved from a domestic craze into a full-blown cultural export powerhouse. According to a 2025 white paper on the development of China's micro-drama industry, the overseas micro-drama market generated a total revenue of over 1.52 billion U.S. dollars between January and August of 2025, marking a year-on-year increase of 194.9 percent. Global downloads of micro-drama apps surged 370.4 percent to approximately 730 million over the same period. Chinese companies dominate the overseas micro-drama market, with 90 percent of the top 20 revenue-generating apps worldwide backed by Chinese origins or investment. Beijing and south China's tech hub Shenzhen have taken the lead in micro-drama exports, housing a cluster of companies spanning content production, platform operations and overseas distribution. Other cities, including Chongqing, Hangzhou in east China, and Chengdu in southwest China, are rapidly catching up by leveraging their strengths in online literature, internet technology and cultural resources. A micro-drama shot at a Chongqing studio and polished through distribution platforms in Beijing or Shenzhen can end up on phone screens in Tokyo, Los Angeles or Jakarta. But winning these markets takes more than just dubbing or subtitling. "Previously, we mostly translated successful domestic shows and sent them out," Zeng said. "Now, more projects are being developed with overseas audiences in mind right from the script stage." In Japan, for instance, Zeng noted that local audiences have shown a strong appetite for stories about women's empowerment and workplace dynamics. As a result, Chinese producers have taken genres already validated in the domestic market and adapted them for Japanese viewers, weaving local social nuances and emotional cues into the narratives. "Going global is no longer just about translating subtitles," Zeng said. "It's about reimagining the entire production chain, from scripts and casting to shooting, post-production workflows and even distribution strategies." "We're moving toward telling stories in a way that local audiences can truly connect with," she added. As high-speed production becomes the industry norm, leading players are moving the competition to a new level. Maiya Media, a digital culture and technology company based in Chongqing, is now seeking to layer its micro-dramas with deeper cultural substance. Its overseas platform, NetShort, has already reached more than 40 countries and regions. To sustain this momentum, the company has also partnered with Sichuan International Studies University in Chongqing to establish a multilingual translation and production base for micro-drama exports, supporting international distribution through talent training in translation and overseas content operations. "We respect local cultures and leverage technology to promote the translation and localization of premium micro-dramas overseas," said He Yunchang, founder and chairman of Maiya Media. "Meanwhile, we hope that overseas audiences will also be able to learn about China's rich culture and contemporary vitality through the characters, scenes and stories in our dramas." ■

item.title: Robot events in China highlight accelerating embodied intelligence innovation through industrial application
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-25
* Humanoid robots shattered human records in the 100-meter and 400-meter races during the ongoing World Humanoid Robot Games held in Beijing from Aug. 22 to 26. With athletic performance steadily improving, robotics entrepreneurs emphasized the necessity to translate robotic prowess into real-world productivity. * China's humanoid robot industry is entering a critical stage of large-scale commercialization and deployment, as embodied intelligence products move from small-batch trials to broader adoption. * The industry's future, many believe, lies not in standalone hardware, but in the integration of three pillars: hardware, embodied AI large models and real-world industrial applications. BEIJING, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- Humanoid robots shattered human records in the 100-meter and 400-meter races during the ongoing World Humanoid Robot Games held in Beijing from Aug. 22 to 26. This marks a striking leap forward from last year's inaugural edition, which left many with memories of viral clips of robots freezing on the starting line or veering off course. With athletic performance steadily improving, robotics entrepreneurs at the event emphasized the necessity to translate robotic prowess into real-world productivity. As purely demonstrative products are unlikely to secure orders, industrial and manufacturing sectors are increasingly expecting robots to deliver tangible results. Reflecting this shift, 21 scenario-based contests are added this year, covering settings such as factories, hotels, homes and logistics facilities. Tasks ranging from industrial assembly and housekeeping to emergency rescue and library book sorting are designed around jobs that can be repetitive, physically demanding, dirty, dangerous, or difficult. FROM DEMOS TO DELIVERABLES Housework is one of the top things people want robots to take on. In housekeeping service contest, robots are tasked to perform a full sequence of housework, including clearing scattered items, folding clothes and putting them in wardrobes, and hanging laundry. These are not easy tasks. "Some objects sit above the counter and can be picked up directly; others are below and require the robot to navigate around obstacles. For humans, this is instinctive, but for robots, it demands different motion algorithms and greater trajectory-planning versatility," said Liu Bingbing, associate professor from Beijing Union University's Robotics College. Challenges sparked solutions. One team developed a lighter structure and materials to improve the robot's motion flexibility. Another team introduced a "lifelong learning mechanism" that enables the robot to continuously adjust its motion programs based on real-time changes in its own joint dynamics -- compensating for wear and hardware variances unique to each unit to maintain stable performance. Despite remaining limitations -- for instance, only a few robots can coordinate both arms to hang clothes on a hanger -- the progress on display still caught the judges' attention. "Last year, most robots could barely fold clothes. After just one year of iteration, they all fold them into neat squares, and then they can open the wardrobe to put clothes away," a judge said. In industrial and agricultural scenarios, some robots have already been deployed in the production process. East China's Hangzhou Electrochemical Group Co., Ltd. has introduced inspection robots to monitor equipment damage and toxic gas leaks in high-temperature, corrosive factory environments. At a tomato farm in Shanghai, dual-arm picking robots have passed field tests for fruit recognition, ripeness grading, and picking sequence planning, ensuring damage-free harvesting. China's humanoid robot industry is entering a critical stage of large-scale commercialization and deployment, as embodied intelligence products move from small-batch trials to broader adoption, Xu Xiaolan, chairwoman of the Chinese Institute of Electronics, said at the 2026 World Robot Conference (WRC). A common question remains for the industry: how to achieve generalized, large-scale deployment of embodied AI across industrial scenarios, so that robots can handle diverse real-world tasks via simple language commands. REAL USE FUELS INNOVATION Xi Yue, co-founder of Robotera, said the industry's near-term path to large-scale deployment lies in controlled, closed-loop scenarios such as logistics, high-end manufacturing and hazardous operations. More complex environments will follow as technologies mature. The core challenge is to build a foundational embodied intelligence system -- one that draws on high-quality real-world data platforms and open-source algorithm ecosystems to strengthen robots' decision-making capabilities and dexterous manipulation skills in dynamic settings, he added. Many robotics firms have already begun deploying their systems in manufacturing and logistics to drive technological progress through hands-on operation. The industry's future, many believe, lies not in standalone hardware, but in the integration of three pillars: hardware, embodied AI foundation models, and real-world industrial applications. At the WRC held from Aug. 19 to Aug. 23 in Beijing, Galbot S1 humanoid robot demonstrated autonomous industrial handling capabilities, including handling, transporting and stacking industrial bins. Powered by Galbot's embodied foundation model, S1 continuously perceives its surroundings, detects environmental changes, and dynamically adjusts its movements based on object positions, task progress and real-time conditions. Galbot S1 has already been deployed in industrial environments, including battery manufacturing facilities at CATL, where it supports demanding workflows requiring high efficiency, precision and reliability. Galbot has also partnered with SAIC Motor and German automotive supplier Bosch to further explore the integration of embodied intelligence into smart manufacturing. The company's technological foundation lies in its embodied foundation model, which integrates perception, decision-making and execution into a unified system. By combining vision-language-action models with world models, the system enables robots to better understand physical environments, reason about the potential outcomes of their actions, and adapt to complex real-world scenarios -- reducing reliance on task-specific programming and fixed workflows. According to Wang He, founder and CTO of Galbot, the company is developing industry-specific vertical models on top of its foundation models. Through a deployment-driven development loop, Galbot performs post-training based on real-world operational data, continuously improving robot performance and enabling more effective deployment across diverse applications. To further accelerate the application-driven innovation cycle, the "Global Robot Application Exploration Program" was launched during this year's WRC. This plan was jointly initiated by the World Robot Cooperation Organization and the Chinese Institute of Electronics, in collaboration with international industry organizations, research institutions and enterprises. The initiative will select 1,000 scenarios annually for free robot trials and secondary development, aiming to bridge the gap between technological breakthroughs and industrial value while fostering an open, win-win global innovation ecosystem. China's embodied intelligence market is also drawing international cooperation opportunities. Jack Perry, chairman of The 48 Group in Britain, noted that China's robotics sector is advancing rapidly, particularly in physical intelligence. Many European companies are considering AI-driven transformation and hope to improve efficiency through robot procurement, he said. Jae Hwan Kim, secretary-general of the Korea Association of AI Robot Industry, highlighted the complementarity between China and ROK. China has solid foundations in large-scale manufacturing, supply chains and AI foundation models, while there exists a vast potential for cooperation between two countries in physical intelligence-driven AI and smart manufacturing, he said. Just as China has called for open and inclusive AI development, the same principle applies to embodied intelligence. Xu called for joint efforts to deepen research on safety and ethics in this field, build a secure, open and inclusive international standard system, and promote mutual recognition of evaluation and certification frameworks. The goal, she said, is to shape a global governance structure with broad consensus -- one that ensures technological progress ultimately serves the well-being of humanity. ■ (Video reporters: Hui Peipei and Meng Jing; video editors: Hui Peipei, Li Qin, Roger Lott and Hong Ling)

item.title: World Insights: Can "Economic D-Day" force Iran into concessions?
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-25
WASHINGTON/TEHRAN, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday unveiled fresh sanctions on Iran and warned countries maintaining economic ties with Tehran of possible secondary sanctions. The campaign amounts to an "Economic D-Day" targeting Iran's global financial links, designed to sever its economic lifelines and push the country toward "complete global isolation and a subsistence economy," according to Bessent. The measures came amid a stalemate after the 60-day negotiating window under a U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding signed in June expired without a final deal or an extension of the temporary ceasefire. With diplomacy stalled, Washington is betting that renewed economic pressure can produce a different outcome. But can greater economic pressure force Tehran to make strategic concessions? A BROADER SQUEEZE In a press release issued on Monday, the U.S. Treasury Department said it had expanded the reach of potential secondary sanctions to five additional sectors -- digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping -- which Washington says Iran relies on to sustain its economy. It also sanctioned nearly 60 entities, individuals and vessels across several jurisdictions over their alleged links to Iran's nuclear and missile procurement, cyber operations and oil-revenue networks. Bessent warned that countries maintaining business ties with Iran could ultimately be forced to choose between those ties and access to the dollar-based financial system, while refusing to identify potential targets or say when penalties might take effect. "We are witnessing a shift from a policy of imposing sanctions on Iran to an attempt to target the network of economic relationships that allows Iran to remain within the global economy for as long as possible," Raad Al-Tal, a professor of economics at the University of Jordan, told Xinhua. Iran has endured U.S. sanctions for decades. But Washington appears to believe that nearly six months of war and a naval blockade have changed the equation. Richard Goldberg, who coordinated efforts to put diplomatic pressure on Iran during Trump's first term, said the combined pressure had created a "perfect storm for capitulation" that had not previously existed. The economic push also offers Washington an alternative to immediate military escalation. Bessent said Thursday the new U.S. policy of "maximum economic pressure" on Iran makes a "large-scale" war less likely. Economics Professor Ying Chen at the New School for Social Research pointed to depleted munitions stockpiles and the approaching midterm elections as two commonly cited reasons for the timing. "If military coercion can't be sustained, economic coercion becomes the natural fallback," she said. WHAT PRESSURE CAN BUY Analysts say a tougher squeeze on Iran's oil exports and financial channels could inflict significant economic damage. Raad Al-Tal said tighter restrictions on oil exports could cut Iran's most important source of revenue. Combined with pressure on the currency, they could raise import costs and inflation, erode purchasing power and place further strain on households, the state budget and the broader economy. Muawiya Al-Toum, a Sudanese expert in diplomacy and international relations, said sustained reductions in oil revenue and access to foreign currency could also constrain Tehran's ability to finance its military and security institutions. But economic damage does not automatically translate into strategic concessions. Abdulaziz Alshaabani, a Saudi researcher at Al Riyadh Center for Political and Strategic Studies, said that economic pressure could push Tehran toward negotiations. Forcing Iran to abandon what it considers "core security interests," however, would be much harder and could be viewed as "strategic surrender rather than compromise," Alshaabani told Xinhua. Jumaa Mohammed, a politics professor at Iraq's Tikrit University, also said that full dismantlement of Iran's nuclear infrastructure would be seen in Tehran as an "outright strategic defeat" that no Iranian leadership was likely to accept. "Nuclear and military decisions aren't calculated purely in economic terms," he further explained, adding that ideological and existential considerations also carry substantial weight. If Iran concludes that Washington's ultimate objective is to eliminate its ability to deter threats or exercise regional influence, Al-Toum said, it may consider enduring sanctions as less dangerous than accepting the proposed settlement. "Whatever the cost of the American sanctions on Iran, this is an existential war for Iran," said Ezzat Saad, director of the Egyptian Council for Foreign Affairs.■

item.title: China warns against unilateral sanctions after U.S. vows "economic asphyxiation" of Iran
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-25
BEIJING, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- China has made clear on multiple occasions that it firmly opposes illegal unilateral sanctions that have no basis in international law and are not authorized by the UN Security Council, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said on Tuesday. Lin made the remarks at a regular news briefing when asked to comment on media reports that U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday laid out plans for the "economic asphyxiation" of Iran, expanding Washington's secondary sanctions threats and warning of dire consequences for countries that do not join the campaign. Economic warfare and maximum pressure do not help solve problems. Instead, they only escalate tensions and conflicts, create spillover risks, disrupt the global economic and financial order, and undermine the legitimate rights and interests of other countries, Lin said. The pressing priority now is to de-escalate the situation and return to the track of dialogue and negotiation as soon as possible, he added. China's cooperation with Iran is always conducted within the framework of international law and should not be disrupted or undermined, Lin said. China is closely following relevant developments and will take all necessary measures to resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests, he noted. ■

item.title: China reports steady consolidation of poverty alleviation gains
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-25
BEIJING, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- China's poverty alleviation outcomes have been steadily consolidated and expanded, with rural per capita income showing a stable rise, a State Council report has revealed. The report on consolidating poverty alleviation achievements and advancing rural revitalization was submitted for deliberation at the ongoing session of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, the country's top legislature, which opened on Tuesday. According to the report, the per capita disposable income of rural residents in counties that have been removed from the poverty list rose from 12,588 yuan (about 1,855 U.S. dollars) in 2020 to 18,627 yuan in 2025, achieving average annual growth of 8.2 percent. It also noted marked improvements in rural infrastructure and public services, and a narrowing development gap compared with other regions. Industrial and employment assistance have been stepped up, and efforts have been made to stabilize jobs for those who have been lifted out of poverty. The number of such people with jobs has exceeded 32 million, the report said. The report also acknowledged persistent challenges, including long-term risks of relapse into poverty and weak development foundations in less-developed areas. Looking ahead, regular assistance will be integrated into the overall rural revitalization strategy, with people at risk of falling back into poverty and underdeveloped regions remaining as the primary targets of assistance. The approach will combine development-oriented support with a sound social security system to safeguard basic livelihoods, the report said. ■

item.title: Roundup: China mulls road safety law revisions, law against cross-border corruption
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-25
Zhao Leji, chairman of the National People's Congress (NPC) Standing Committee, presides over the first plenary meeting of the 24th session of the 14th NPC Standing Committee at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, capital of China, Aug. 25, 2026. (Xinhua/Pang Xinglei) BEIJING, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- Chinese lawmakers convened on Tuesday to review a raft of bills, including draft revisions to the Road Traffic Safety Law, a draft law on combating cross-border corruption and a draft healthcare security law. The bills were submitted for deliberation at the 24th session of the Standing Committee of the 14th National People's Congress (NPC), the country's top legislature. Zhao Leji, chairman of the NPC Standing Committee, presided over the first plenary meeting of the session. In the meeting, lawmakers deliberated a draft healthcare security law. Submitted for a third reading, the draft includes provisions on long-term care insurance, aiming to further protect the rights and interests of insured people. A draft law on farmland protection and quality improvement was submitted for its third reading, adding provisions on talent cultivation and strengthening oversight of funds for high-standard farmland development. Lawmakers also reviewed a revised draft of the Agriculture Law, which improves support for agricultural and rural economic development, enhances protection for farmers' rights and interests, and strengthens rural development and governance. A draft revision to the National Defense Mobilization Law was submitted for its second reading. The revisions clarify the concept of national defense mobilization and rules on the collection, use and security management of relevant data. Lawmakers reviewed a draft amendment to the lawyers law that improves the provisions to boost foreign-related legal services. A revised draft of the Enterprise Bankruptcy Law, submitted for its second reading, refines rules on the bankruptcy of individual debtors bearing joint and several liability, improves the reorganization system, and adjusts the priority order for distributions from the bankruptcy estate. Also under review was a revised draft of the banking supervision and regulation law, which introduces classified and tiered supervision of banking institutions, improves the system for protecting banking consumers' rights and interests, and adds a separate chapter on risk resolution. Lawmakers also reviewed a revised draft of the Water Law. The second-reading draft strengthens provisions on the protection of water resources and water ecology, national water network development, and water conservation and recycling. Draft revisions to the Road Traffic Safety Law were submitted for review, seeking to improve the road traffic safety management system and strengthen the legal framework for maintaining traffic order. The draft includes a dedicated chapter on autonomous vehicles. A draft law on combating cross-border corruption was submitted for the first reading, aiming to prevent and punish transnational corruption, deepen international cooperation and safeguard national sovereignty, security, and development interests. Lawmakers also heard a series of reports, including a report on the implementation of the 2026 plan for national economic and social development, a report on budget execution, a report on government debt management in 2025, and a supervisory research report on government debt management in 2025. A report on improving the quality of cultural products and services and a report on efforts to consolidate and expand achievements in poverty alleviation and advance all-around rural revitalization were also on the agenda of the lawmakers. Lawmakers also deliberated an extradition treaty between China and Hungary, a deputy qualification report and personnel-related bills. ■

item.title: Xi stresses consolidating, expanding campaign on correct view of governance performance
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
BEIJING, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, has emphasized the importance of consolidating and expanding the progress made in a Party-wide study and education campaign for establishing and practicing a correct understanding of governance performance. Xi, also Chinese president and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks in a recent instruction, which was studied at a meeting of the CPC Central Leading Group for Party Building held on Monday. Xi stressed that establishing and putting into practice a correct view of governance performance is a long-term task that requires sustained efforts. Since the 18th CPC National Congress, the organization of study and education campaigns across the Party to address major and pressing issues in Party building has become an important institutional arrangement, Xi said, lauding the notable results achieved in the latest campaign. Xi emphasized the need to regularly conduct education on the correct view of governance performance, guiding Party members and officials to always take responsibility, perform their duties and fulfill their obligations in accordance with such a view. Efforts should also be made to improve differentiated assessment and evaluation systems, and establish a personnel selection and appointment orientation that values solid work and concrete results, Xi said. During the meeting, participants thoroughly studied and implemented Xi's instruction, reviewed the campaign, and made arrangements for consolidating and expanding the campaign's outcomes and establishing a long-term mechanism accordingly. The meeting was chaired by Cai Qi, who is head of the CPC Central Leading Group for Party Building, and was also attended by Li Xi, the group's deputy head. Cai and Li, both of whom are members of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee, also delivered speeches. The meeting noted that the campaign has resolved prominent issues related to deviations in view of governance performance, regulated the official conduct of leading officials at all levels, and given a strong boost to all work aimed at ensuring a good start to the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030). The campaign, which started in late February, has basically concluded and aimed to correct misguided views on governance that often breed vanity projects, hidden risks, heavy burdens on local communities, and public discontent. ■
